chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya from Abu Abdillah al-Razi from Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Abi Nasr from al-Mashriqi from Abu al-Hasan (peace be upon him) who said:
I asked him about eating al-murri and al-kamakh, and I said that it is made from wheat and barley, so we eat it. He said, 'Yes, it is permissible, and we eat it.'
From him (Muhammad ibn Yahya) from al-Hasan ibn Ali al-Hamdani from al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Mad'ani who said:
I asked him about sikanjabin, gallab, mulberry syrup, quince syrup, apple syrup, and pomegranate syrup, and he wrote, 'Permissible.'
Muhammad ibn Ya'qub from a number of our companions from Sahl ibn Ziyad from Mansur ibn al-Abbas from Ja'far ibn Ahmad al-Makfuuf who said:
I wrote to him, meaning Abu al-Hasan al-Awwal (peace be upon him), asking him about sikanjabin, gallab, mulberry syrup, apple syrup, and pomegranate syrup, and he wrote, 'Permissible.'
From him from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Hamdan ibn Sulayman from Ali ibn al-Hasan from Ja'far ibn Ahmad al-Makfuuf:

Like the first, and added to it and mulberry syrup, and after that, if the one who sells them is not an expert, and they are sold in our markets, he wrote, 'It is permissible, there is no harm with them.'

key_terms.السِّكَنْجَبِينِ: Sikanjabin, a vinegar-based syrup or drink.
key_terms.الْكَامَخِ: A type of food or condiment, often associated with grains.
key_terms.الْمُرِّيِّ: A type of food or condiment, often associated with grains.

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on eating murri, kamakh, and various fruit syrups?
ai.summary: These narrations from the Tahdhib al-Ahkam highlight the Shia scholarly principle of 'original permissibility' (al-asl fi al-aklay al-halal), confirming that common grain-based foods and fruit syrups (rub) are inherently halal unless proven otherwise. The inclusion of a specific condition for market goods sold by non-experts reflects the practical juristic concern for consumer protection and the reliability of commercial transactions in the Abbasid era. This underscores the flexibility of Shia fiqh in accommodating everyday dietary practices while maintaining rigorous standards for food safety and authenticity.
